subject: Cognitive Science
title: Appeal to Authority
description: A micro-lesson that makes Appeal to Authority usable.

hook.text: A famous actor endorses a health supplement. He knows nothing about medicine. But people trust him anyway.

buildup.text: Appeal to authority: accepting a claim because an authority figure supports it, regardless of their expertise.

discovery.text: It's only a fallacy when the authority is outside their domain. A climatologist on climate isn't fallacious.

twist.text: Even real experts can be wrong. Authority makes a claim more probable, not certain.

climax.text: Evaluate the evidence, not the source. Good evidence from a no-name beats bad evidence from a celebrity.

punchline.text: Famous doesn't mean right. Credentials don't mean certain.

quiz.question: When is an appeal to authority a fallacy?
options: When the authority is outside their area of expertise
Every time someone cites an expert

details.summary: An appeal to authority uses an expert's opinion as evidence rather than engaging with the actual reasoning or evidence. While expert opinions are useful starting points, they are not proof. Experts can be wrong, biased, or speaking outside their area of genuine expertise.
details.whyItMatters: Appeals to authority are tricky because experts are often right. The fallacy lies in using their authority as a substitute for evaluating the actual evidence.
takeaways: Expert opinion is useful but not a substitute for evidence
Experts can be wrong or speak outside their true expertise
Evaluate the argument, not just who is making it

faq.question: When is citing an authority legitimate?
faq.answer: Citing authority is legitimate when the expert is speaking within their field of expertise, when there is broad consensus among experts, and when you cannot evaluate the evidence yourself.

faq.question: How do you evaluate expert claims critically?
faq.answer: Check whether the expert is speaking within their actual field. Look for consensus: one dissenting expert does not refute a field. Ask whether they have conflicts of interest. Look for the evidence behind their claim, not just the claim itself. Expert consensus on evidence is the gold standard.
